text: Defect means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product.

metadata.title: Section 2(10) - Definition of Defect

text: Deficiency means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service.

metadata.title: Section 2(11) - Definition of Deficiency
metadata.legal_purpose: Defines actionable shortcomings in professional, commercial, or public services.

text: Misleading advertisement in relation to any product or service means an advertisement, which falsely describes such product or service, or gives a false guarantee to, or is likely to mislead the consumers as to the nature, substance, quantity or quality of such product or service.

metadata.title: Section 2(28) - Definition of Misleading Advertisement
metadata.legal_purpose: Prohibits deceptive sales marketing, false guarantees, or scientific misrepresentations.

text: Unfair trade practice means a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice including making false or misleading representation, refusal to refund paid consideration within 30 days, or disclosing confidential personal information.

metadata.title: Section 2(47) - Definition of Unfair Trade Practice
metadata.legal_purpose: Establishes comprehensive prohibition against deceptive commercial conduct and mandatory 30-day refund rules.

text: Where the District Commission is satisfied that the goods complained against suffer from any of the defects specified in the complaint or that any of the allegations contained in the complaint about services or unfair trade practices are proved, it shall issue an order directing the opposite party to remove defects, replace goods with defect-free items, return the price paid along with interest, or pay compensation.

metadata.title: Section 39 - Findings of District Commission and Statutory Orders

text: A product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer, product service provider, or product seller for any harm caused on account of a defective product. A product manufacturer shall be liable if the product contains a manufacturing defect, design defect, or non-conformance with express warranty.

metadata.title: Section 83 & 84 - Product Liability Action and Manufacturer Liability

text: A product liability action cannot be brought against the product seller or manufacturer if at the time of harm the product was misused, altered, or modified by the consumer, or if the danger was obvious or commonly known.

metadata.title: Section 87 - Exceptions to Product Liability Action

text: Marketplace e-commerce entities shall display clear details about return, refund, exchange, delivery, shipment, modes of payment, grievance redressal mechanism, and seller details to consumers.

metadata.title: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 - Rule 5: Liabilities of Marketplace E-Commerce Entities

text:
Tata Motors Ltd. vs. Antonio Paulo Vaz & Anr. ((2021) 4 SCC 300)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: The consumer purchased a brand-new car manufactured by Tata Motors from an authorized dealership. Within days of delivery, the vehicle experienced severe mechanical breakdown and engine stalling. The dealer attempted repairs multiple times without success and refused to refund the purchase price or replace the vehicle.
Issues: Whether a brand-new vehicle suffering from major breakdown within days constitutes a manufacturing defect under Consumer Protection Law?; Whether the product manufacturer can avoid vicarious product liability by citing principal-to-principal dealer contracts?

metadata.consumer_supporting_principle: Inherent manufacturing defects in new goods entitle the consumer to full refund or replacement under Section 39.
metadata.respondent_supporting_principle: Manufacturers are liable for replacement only when independent mechanical evidence proves an unrepairable manufacturing defect.
metadata.decision: Complaint Allowed in favour of the Consumer.
metadata.relief: Ordered refund of the full purchase price of ₹8,50,000 along with 9% interest per annum from the date of purchase, plus ₹50,000 as compensation for mental agony and litigation costs.

text:
Tata Motors Ltd. vs. Antonio Paulo Vaz & Anr. ((2021) 4 SCC 300)
Consumer Position: The consumer argued that purchasing a brand-new vehicle that breaks down immediately constitutes an inherent manufacturing defect under Section 2(10), violating statutory quality warranties and entitling the buyer to a full refund with interest.
Defense Position: Tata Motors argued that the relationship between the manufacturer and the dealer was on a principal-to-principal basis and that the consumer should only be granted free repair of specific parts under warranty clauses rather than a vehicle replacement.
Consumer Principle: Inherent manufacturing defects in new goods entitle the consumer to full refund or replacement under Section 39.
Respondent Principle: Manufacturers are liable for replacement only when independent mechanical evidence proves an unrepairable manufacturing defect.

Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh (2022 NCDRC 412)
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: The consumer ordered a high-end laptop on an online e-commerce marketplace platform during a sale. Upon opening the sealed package, the consumer received a brick instead of the laptop. Amazon refused to process a refund or replacement, claiming that the seller was a third-party entity and Amazon was merely an intermediary platform exempt from liability.
Issues: Whether an e-commerce marketplace platform can claim intermediary immunity when a wrong/defective product is delivered?; Whether non-refund by an online platform constitutes an Unfair Trade Practice under Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020?

metadata.title: Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh - Facts & Issues
metadata.case_name: Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh
metadata.court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
metadata.facts_summary: The consumer ordered a high-end laptop on an online e-commerce marketplace platform during a sale. Upon opening the sealed package, the consumer received a brick instead of the laptop. Amazon refused to process a refund or replacement, claiming that the seller was a third-party entity and Amazon was merely an intermediary platform exempt from liability.
metadata.consumer_supporting_principle: E-commerce platforms handling payments and fulfillment are accountable for non-delivery or wrong product delivery under Section 2(47) and E-Commerce Rules.
metadata.respondent_supporting_principle: Pure intermediary platforms that do not manufacture or pack goods are exempt if prompt refund action is directed against the actual third-party seller.
metadata.decision: Revision Petition dismissed; Order against E-Commerce Platform Upheld.
metadata.relief: Ordered immediate refund of ₹74,999 with 12% interest, plus ₹25,000 compensation and ₹10,000 litigation expenses.

text:
Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh (2022 NCDRC 412)
Consumer Position: The consumer submitted that payment was collected by Amazon and the delivery was fulfilled by Amazon's logistics network. Denying a refund for a missing/tampered product amounts to severe deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
Defense Position: Amazon contended that under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, it enjoys safe harbour status as an intermediary and is not liable for seller misrepresentation.
Consumer Principle: E-commerce platforms handling payments and fulfillment are accountable for non-delivery or wrong product delivery under Section 2(47) and E-Commerce Rules.
Respondent Principle: Pure intermediary platforms that do not manufacture or pack goods are exempt if prompt refund action is directed against the actual third-party seller.

text:
Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh (2022 NCDRC 412)
Court Reasoning: The NCDRC ruled that under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, marketplace platforms that handle payment collection, logistics, and customer interface cannot disown responsibility for fraudulent non-delivery or defective shipments. Relief Awarded: Ordered immediate refund of ₹74,999 with 12% interest, plus ₹25,000 compensation and ₹10,000 litigation expenses.

Horlicks Ltd. vs. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. (2018 SCC OnLine Del 12975)
Court: Delhi High Court
Facts: The defendant published comparative television and print advertisements claiming that one cup of Complan was equivalent to two cups of Horlicks in terms of growth protein, asserting '2x Faster Growth'. The claims were published without clinical validation standards acceptable under consumer advertising guidelines.
Issues: Whether published commercial advertisements making unverified comparative performance claims constitute Misleading Advertisements under Consumer Law?; What evidentiary standards are required to prove a scientific growth claim made to public consumers?

The claims were published without clinical validation standards acceptable under consumer advertising guidelines.
metadata.consumer_supporting_principle: Unsubstantiated scientific growth promises in mass advertisements violate consumer rights to accurate product information.
metadata.respondent_supporting_principle: Truthful commercial puffery comparing nutritional values is permissible unless proven demonstrably false.
metadata.decision: Injunction Granted against the Misleading Advertisement.

Indian Medical Association vs. V.P. Shantha & Ors. ((1995) 6 SCC 651)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: A landmark medical negligence dispute where medical practitioners claimed that medical treatment provided by doctors does not fall within the scope of 'service' under consumer protection law, and patients cannot be treated as 'consumers'.
Issues: Whether medical services rendered by medical practitioners and hospitals fall under 'service' under Section 2(42) of Consumer Protection Law?; Whether patients paying fees for medical treatment qualify as consumers entitled to claim compensation for medical deficiency?

metadata.respondent_supporting_principle: Free medical services rendered in government hospitals without consideration are excluded from consumer commission jurisdiction.
metadata.decision: Landmark Ruling in favor of Consumer Protection Scope.
metadata.relief: Affirmed the jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions to hear medical deficiency complaints and award compensation for medical negligence.

Lucknow Development Authority vs. M.K. Gupta ((1994) 1 SCC 243)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: A homebuyer deposited complete installments for a residential flat allotted by a public housing development authority. The authority failed to deliver possession of the flat for over 7 years beyond the agreed timeline and refused to pay interest or refund the money.
Issues: Whether statutory development authorities providing housing plots/flats perform a 'service' under Consumer Law?; Whether inordinate delay in handing over possession of real estate constitutes Deficiency in Service entitling the homebuyer to refund with interest?

State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan (2020 NCDRC 301)
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: Unauthorised fraudulent ATM withdrawals took place from the consumer's bank account without OTP generation or SMS alerts sent to the mobile number. The bank refused to credit the fraudulently debited amount, claiming customer negligence in safeguarding PIN.
Issues: Whether failure of a bank to send real-time SMS alerts and prevent unauthorized electronic transactions constitutes Deficiency in Service under Consumer Law?; Who bears the burden of proof for unauthorized banking transactions under RBI Circulars and Consumer Law?

metadata.title: State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan - Facts & Issues
metadata.case_name: State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan
metadata.court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
metadata.facts_summary: Unauthorised fraudulent ATM withdrawals took place from the consumer's bank account without OTP generation or SMS alerts sent to the mobile number. The bank refused to credit the fraudulently debited amount, claiming customer negligence in safeguarding PIN.
metadata.consumer_supporting_principle: Unauthorized electronic bank debits notified within 3 days carry zero liability for the consumer under Section 2(11).
metadata.respondent_supporting_principle: Banks are not liable if documentary ATM log evidence proves PIN compromised directly by customer negligence.
metadata.decision: Order in favor of Account Holder.
metadata.relief: Ordered State Bank of India to reverse the fraudulent debit of ₹1,20,000 with 9% interest and pay ₹20,000 compensation.

text:
State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan (2020 NCDRC 301)
Consumer Position: The account holder immediately notified the bank within 24 hours. Under RBI Zero Liability Guidelines, the consumer bears zero liability for third-party security breaches.
Defense Position: The bank argued that ATM transactions require physical card insertion and PIN entry, implying consumer disclosure of PIN.
Consumer Principle: Unauthorized electronic bank debits notified within 3 days carry zero liability for the consumer under Section 2(11).
Respondent Principle: Banks are not liable if documentary ATM log evidence proves PIN compromised directly by customer negligence.

Judgment: Clause triage: arbitration.

Legal area: Arbitration.

Primary risks: check overbreadth, internal inconsistency, remedy mismatch, enforceability concerns, and conflict with other clauses. Do not approve this clause in isolation.

Documents/context needed: contract, interim relief evidence, claim documents, arbitration clause, seat/venue details.

Review questions: Who bears the commercial risk? Are fraud, wilful misconduct, confidentiality breach, IP infringement, data loss, unpaid fees, statutory liability, and third-party claims carved out where needed? Does the clause match insurance, pricing, bargaining position, and governing law?

Suggested edit direction: narrow the clause to the actual transaction risk, add balanced carve-outs, align it with dispute resolution and termination, and create a clear evidence trail.

Citation rule: cite only verified contract provisions, statutes, or case law supplied by counsel.

Fact pattern: a marketplace seller uses a confusingly similar product photographs.

Potential routes: copyright for original expression, trademark or passing off for brand/source confusion, design/patent only if registration and subject matter support it, contract claim if an agreement controls ownership or confidentiality, and platform takedown as a fast non-litigation route.

Evidence pack: domain and social handle records, invoices and publication history, registration certificates or applications, assignment/licence agreements, source/design files, screenshots with URL and timestamp.

Output for counsel: prepare a rights chart with asset, owner, proof, infringement theory, forum, interim relief possibility, and citation/source status. Do not cite cases unless verified.

Potential routes: copyright for original expression, trademark or passing off for brand/source confusion, design/patent only if registration and subject matter support it, contract claim if an agreement controls ownership or confidentiality, and platform takedown as a fast non-litigation route.

Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) / Court
Facts: Review this clause for an Indian legal team and identify triage risks, not final advice.
Issues: contract
Provisions: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Judgment: Clause type: Contract and commercial disputes risk review.

Main risks: The clause may be one-sided, internally inconsistent, or too broad for the commercial purpose. It should be tested against the rest of the agreement, the transaction value, data/security exposure, IP ownership chain, dispute-resolution clause, and applicable Indian law.

Questions for counsel: Which party controls the relevant documents? Are there carve-outs for fraud, confidentiality breach, IP infringement, data loss, wilful misconduct, statutory liability, and payment obligations? Does the clause conflict with another clause such as indemnity, jurisdiction, arbitration, termination, or audit rights?

Suggested negotiation position: make the clause specific, add sensible carve-outs, align it with insurance/commercial risk, and avoid language that makes the remedy illusory.

Citation note: Do not cite cases or sections unless the governing contract, statute, or verified legal source is provided.

Judgment: Clause triage: warranty disclaimer.

Legal area: Contracts and commercial disputes.

Primary risks: check overbreadth, internal inconsistency, remedy mismatch, enforceability concerns, and conflict with other clauses. Do not approve this clause in isolation.

Documents/context needed: termination notice, emails, invoices, agreement, delivery proof.

Review questions: Who bears the commercial risk? Are fraud, wilful misconduct, confidentiality breach, IP infringement, data loss, unpaid fees, statutory liability, and third-party claims carved out where needed? Does the clause match insurance, pricing, bargaining position, and governing law?

Suggested edit direction: narrow the clause to the actual transaction risk, add balanced carve-outs, align it with dispute resolution and termination, and create a clear evidence trail.

Citation rule: cite only verified contract provisions, statutes, or case law supplied by counsel.

Judgment: IP triage result: Do not treat this as one single IP claim yet. Split the matter into ownership, protectable subject matter, proof of copying/access, commercial harm, and remedy.

Fact pattern: a marketplace seller uses a confusingly similar product photographs.

Potential routes: copyright for original expression, trademark or passing off for brand/source confusion, design/patent only if registration and subject matter support it, contract claim if an agreement controls ownership or confidentiality, and platform takedown as a fast non-litigation route.

Evidence pack: invoices and publication history, assignment/licence agreements, domain and social handle records, source/design files, screenshots with URL and timestamp, registration certificates or applications.

Questions to ask: Who created the asset? Was there an assignment? Was the asset published before? Is there registration? Is the allegedly copied material an idea, function, or original expression? Can access and similarity be shown?

Output for counsel: prepare a rights chart with asset, owner, proof, infringement theory, forum, interim relief possibility, and citation/source status. Do not cite cases unless verified.

text:
Title: Horlicks Ltd. vs. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd.
Court: Delhi High Court
Facts: The defendant published comparative television and print advertisements claiming that one cup of Complan was equivalent to two cups of Horlicks in terms of growth protein, asserting '2x Faster Growth'. The claims were published without clinical validation standards acceptable under consumer advertising guidelines.
Issues: Whether published commercial advertisements making unverified comparative performance claims constitute Misleading Advertisements under Consumer Law? | What evidentiary standards are required to prove a scientific growth claim made to public consumers?
Provisions: Section 2(28), Section 10 & 18
Judgment: The Court held that commercial speech does not extend to making false or misleading representations regarding health or nutritional benefits. Advertisements that claim specific measurable outcomes (e.g. 2x growth) must be supported by proper scientific testing, failing which they constitute misleading advertisements under Section 2(28). Injunction Granted against the Misleading Advertisement.

text:
Title: State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: Unauthorised fraudulent ATM withdrawals took place from the consumer's bank account without OTP generation or SMS alerts sent to the mobile number. The bank refused to credit the fraudulently debited amount, claiming customer negligence in safeguarding PIN.
Issues: Whether failure of a bank to send real-time SMS alerts and prevent unauthorized electronic transactions constitutes Deficiency in Service under Consumer Law? | Who bears the burden of proof for unauthorized banking transactions under RBI Circulars and Consumer Law?
Provisions: Section 2(11), Section 39(1)(d)
Judgment: The NCDRC held that banking institutions owe a strict duty of care to implement secure electronic payment systems. Where unauthorized transactions occur without SMS alert dispatch, the bank cannot penalize the account holder. Failure to credit zero-liability fraud within 10 days is a clear deficiency in service. Order in favor of Account Holder.

text:
Title: Lucknow Development Authority vs. M.K. Gupta
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: A homebuyer deposited complete installments for a residential flat allotted by a public housing development authority. The authority failed to deliver possession of the flat for over 7 years beyond the agreed timeline and refused to pay interest or refund the money.
Issues: Whether statutory development authorities providing housing plots/flats perform a 'service' under Consumer Law? | Whether inordinate delay in handing over possession of real estate constitutes Deficiency in Service entitling the homebuyer to refund with interest?
Provisions: Section 2(42), Section 39(1)(d)
Judgment: The Supreme Court held that housing construction and real estate development are express statutory services under consumer law. Public bodies cannot misbehave or cause unjust delay without accountability. Inordinate delay in possession is a classic deficiency in service. Appeal Dismissed; Ruling in favor of Homebuyer.

text:
Title: Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: The consumer ordered a high-end laptop on an online e-commerce marketplace platform during a sale. Upon opening the sealed package, the consumer received a brick instead of the laptop. Amazon refused to process a refund or replacement, claiming that the seller was a third-party entity and Amazon was merely an intermediary platform exempt from liability.
Issues: Whether an e-commerce marketplace platform can claim intermediary immunity when a wrong/defective product is delivered? | Whether non-refund by an online platform constitutes an Unfair Trade Practice under Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020?
Provisions: Rule 4 & Rule 6, Section 2(47), Section 86
Judgment: The NCDRC ruled that under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, marketplace platforms that handle payment collection, logistics, and customer interface cannot disown responsibility for fraudulent non-delivery or defective shipments. Safe harbour under the IT Act does not override explicit duties under consumer protection law. Revision Petition dismissed; Order against E-Commerce Platform Upheld.

text:
Title: FIITJEE Ltd. vs. Minathi Rath
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: A student enrolled in a 2-year coaching program and paid the full fee upfront. Due to unsatisfactory teaching standards, the student left the course within 3 months. The institute refused to refund the remaining 21 months' fee, citing a non-refundable clause in the enrollment agreement.
Issues: Whether coaching institutes collecting advance non-refundable fees for multi-year courses commit an Unfair Trade Practice? | Whether non-refund of unavailed course fee when a student leaves midway constitutes Deficiency in Service?
Provisions: Section 2(47), Section 2(46)
Judgment: The NCDRC held that educational coaching institutions cannot collect advance fees for the entire duration of multi-year courses and retain unearned money. One-sided non-refundable clauses signed under compulsion are 'unfair contracts'. Institutes are entitled only to retain pro-rata fee for the period attended. Revision Petition of Coaching Institute Dismissed.

text:
Title: Tata Motors Ltd. vs. Antonio Paulo Vaz & Anr.
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: The consumer purchased a brand-new car manufactured by Tata Motors from an authorized dealership. Within days of delivery, the vehicle experienced severe mechanical breakdown and engine stalling. The dealer attempted repairs multiple times without success and refused to refund the purchase price or replace the vehicle.
Issues: Whether a brand-new vehicle suffering from major breakdown within days constitutes a manufacturing defect under Consumer Protection Law? | Whether the product manufacturer can avoid vicarious product liability by citing principal-to-principal dealer contracts?
Provisions: Section 2(10), Section 39(1)(b)(c), Section 84
Judgment: The Supreme Court held that delivering a brand-new vehicle with severe mechanical defects constitutes a fundamental breach of statutory consumer rights. Where a product suffers from an inherent manufacturing defect that cannot be rectified by routine repairs, forcing the consumer to accept a repaired car is unfair. The manufacturer and dealer are jointly liable. Complaint Allowed in favour of the Consumer.
